doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Effects of the merger: integrated bands but lost representation
summary: The 49ers band integrates and clubs hire mixed bands, but black musicians lost their officers and convention votes.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: When the merger happened, was it a positive thing immediately or at all?

Well yes, on one hand it was positive. The 49er band, they got integrated. Because the 49ers, our football team, they were playing at Keesar Stadium then. That was out in the park. And they had a forty piece band and the band became integrated. And then of course by then, by 1960, many of the clubs like the Black Hawk, they were hiring traveling bands and local bands, and many of the clubs, they hired mixed bands. In a way you know you figure — Al Forbes, our Secretary/Treasurer/Business Agent, the one that took my five bucks — that was his dream. Because integration, even under Martin Luther King, integration they figured, that was the greater good. But for us well we lost our representation. We lost our official family. Our President, Secretary/Treasurer/Business Agent, the Board of Directors, that all went by the wayside you see. Also we lost our representation at the American Federation of Musicians’ Conference, the conference they give every year, convention. In that way you lost representation and we’ve never been able to integrate the symphony. They have Asians, but we don’t have any black people, African-Americans, in our symphony. The ballet we had a marvelous conductor, Denis deCoteau, but he passed away. The ballet orchestra — well we had Elaine Jones on tympani, she was in the symphony for a very short while.
